title: Auri user docs
heading: Auri user docs
text: Auri turns money into real allocated gold that you own, then lets that gold do work: borrow cash against it without selling, send it to family, or buy a little every week automatically. These pages document what the app does today, number by number — what each action costs, what it changes, what can go wrong, and when not to do it at all.

title: Auri user docs
heading: What Auri is, in 60 seconds
text: When you buy, your money becomes USDC on the Arbitrum network and is swapped for tokenized gold . The gold is Tether Gold; on Arbitrum the token you hold is XAUt0 ( 0x40461291347e1eCbb09499F3371D3f17f10d7159 ), backed one-for-one by native XAUt on Ethereum, itself backed by one troy ounce of vaulted physical gold per token. It lands in a self-custody vault whose address you can see in your profile. Amounts display in your chosen currency; settlement is in USDC. Once you hold gold you can borrow dollars against it instead of selling. Auri posts your gold as collateral in a public lending market on Morpho (Arbitrum One) and hands you USDC. Nothing is sold, and anyone can inspect that market at app.morpho.org . The rate floats : that market sets it minute to minute, not Auri. Auri charges 0.49% to buy gold and 0.49% to sell, and covers the network fee, so you never need a gas token. Every other fee, minimum and limit lives in Reference . Not live yet. The Auri card is a waitlist, not a product — you can join the queue, you cannot spend gold today. Cross-border remittance is also not live. Wherever these appear they are labelled Coming soon , and no page gives you steps for them. Buy gold own the asset Borrow against it liquidity without selling Spend or invest put the cash to work Repay gold stays yours throughout Your gold stays in your vault when you borrow — only the stablecoin leg moves.

title: Auri user docs
heading: Is Auri right for you?
text: Gold has no cash flow: no dividend, no interest, no earnings. It pays you only if someone later pays more than you did, so the question is not "what will this return" but "what do I want to hold instead of cash". Three patterns cover most people here. You want savings that aren't entirely in your own currency Read Start here , then Buy gold , then set a small recurring buy in Auto-Invest — from as little as $10 a cycle. Read Trust and proof before the balance gets large. You need cash and don't want to sell Selling ends your gold position and may create a taxable disposal; borrowing keeps the position and creates an obligation instead. Read Borrowing strategies first, then Borrow against your gold and Repay . You want to put gold in someone else's hands Gold is a durable gift rather than money that gets spent, and grams read as a gift where a dollar figure reads as a transfer. See Gift and send gold . When Auri is the wrong tool You are carrying high-interest debt. Paying it down beats any expected gold return, and it is certain. You need the money within twelve months. Gold can be down when your deadline arrives, and exiting costs 0.49%. You are buying because the price just went up. You want to borrow for something your income cannot repay, or you cannot check your position weekly. See Risks .

title: Auri user docs
heading: Everyday actions
text: The four things most people do in a normal month. Each page states cost, time and reversibility before the steps. Buy gold — buy from your cash balance or a funding rail, in dollars, grams, troy ounces or XAUT, and read the confirmation screen well enough to catch a bad one. Add and withdraw cash — fund your account and take money out: bank transfer in the US, Interac e-Transfer in Canada, debit card, or USDC from a wallet you control. Gift and send gold — send gold by username, to a wallet address, or as a claim link to someone with no account, and manage a gift nobody has claimed. Auto-Invest — run a daily, weekly or monthly recurring buy, pause, resize or stop it, and see what a recurring buy does not protect you from. The constraint that surprises people. Once you borrow, part of your gold becomes locked collateral, and locked gold cannot be sold, gifted or sent until you repay or unlock it. The app tracks free and locked balances separately and blocks outbound actions above the free amount: locked versus free gold .

title: Auri user docs
heading: Borrowing
text: Borrowing is the part of Auri where you can lose gold you already own, so it gets the most detailed treatment. Borrow against your gold — take a loan in USDC, size it deliberately instead of accepting the maximum, and read your loan-to-value, health factor and liquidation price. Repay and unlock — repay from cash, watch your loan-to-value fall, and unlock collateral so gold is free to move again. Unlocking is its own action, not an automatic consequence of repaying. Read this before you borrow: Borrowing strategies — borrow or sell, how to choose a loan-to-value and why the maximum on offer is never the right answer, what your buffer is worth in dollars and percent, the three ways out of a loan, and when not to borrow at all. Liquidation, plainly. The lending market Auri uses has an on-chain liquidation loan-to-value of 77% — a line to stay well clear of, not a target. If gold falls far enough for your loan to reach it, part of your gold is sold to repay the loan, and you do not choose the moment. Your liquidation price, health factor and buffer are shown live in the app: how liquidation works .

title: Auri user docs
heading: Advanced
text: Boost (leverage) — borrow against gold, buy more gold with the proceeds, repeat to a chosen multiplier, then manage or partly close the position. Shows the amplified gain and loss on identical numbers, and how much closer liquidation moves at each multiplier. Boost is gated, and should be. It appears only after you switch on Pro mode, cannot be open alongside a standard loan, and refuses multipliers that push your loan-to-value too near liquidation. Leverage magnifies losses as reliably as gains, and costs a floating rate to hold even in a flat market. If you have not read how liquidation works , you are not ready for it.

title: Auri user docs
heading: Trust and safety
text: For a product that converts savings into metal you will never touch, "where is it and how do I check" comes before "how do I buy". Trust, custody and proof — follow the chain from your token to a physical bar, check the live lending market yourself, and understand what the published attestations do and do not prove. Risks — the full list in plain language: price risk, liquidation, floating rates, smart-contract and bridge risk, custody risk, irreversible transfers, and the risks created by your own devices.

text: The landing page carries two calculators that use the same arithmetic as the app: how much gold an amount buys, and — from your gold value and loan size — your loan-to-value, monthly interest, liquidation price and how far gold must fall to reach it. Money examples are in US dollars unless a rail is genuinely regional — Interac e-Transfer is Canada-only. title: Start here
heading: Why a small first buy is the right first buy
text: Gold is a store of value, not an income asset. No dividend, no interest, no earnings — the whole return is the price, and the price can fall for years at a stretch. Most people hold it as insurance against their own currency, not because they expect it to outperform. That tells you what to measure on day one: whether you can hold the position calmly, not whether it rose this week. A small first buy buys information no documentation can: how long your rail really takes, how the price you got compares with the price you saw, and how you feel when the position is down a few dollars. Those answers tell you whether a larger amount is appropriate. The experiment costs 49 cents at US$100; at US$10,000 it costs US$49 and much more anxiety. When buying gold is the wrong move. If you carry high-interest debt, paying it down is a guaranteed return gold cannot promise. If you need the money inside a year, a volatile asset is the wrong container. If you are buying mainly because the price just rose, wait a week. Auri will not tell you what share of your savings belongs in gold, and be wary of anyone who does. The full accounting is on risks — read it before your second buy.

title: Start here
heading: If something does not look right
text: The code never arrives. Resend once, check spam, then switch identifier or use a passkey — a passkey needs no code. The buy says pending. Bank transfers credit on settlement, typically one to two business days. Expand the Activity row to see which leg it waits on. Verification failed. Usually glare, a cropped edge, or a name mismatch. Retake flat under indirect light; enter your legal name exactly as printed. The ounces look wrong. Recompute: amount minus 0.49%, divided by the review-screen price. If it still differs, the price moved — the review screen quotes, it does not lock. You sent USDC on the wrong network. Only send USDC on Arbitrum. Other tokens or networks may be unrecoverable — no support ticket reverses a blockchain transfer. Auri can never approve a transaction for you. Anything leaving your account later — sending, gifting, moving gold to an external wallet — needs a second confirmation from you, by passkey or two 6-digit codes. Treat any message asking for a code as an attack.

title: Buying gold
heading: Buying gold
text: Buying gold in Auri converts money you already hold into tokenised gold that lands in a vault only you control. When you finish you own a specific weight of gold — divisible to a millionth of a troy ounce — that you can hold, send, gift or borrow against without selling. This page covers the flow tap by tap, what it actually costs, what you end up owning, and when buying is the wrong move.

title: Buying gold
heading: Why people do this
text: Most people buy for one of three reasons: they want savings held in something other than their home currency, they want a hard asset without a safe or a dealer, or they want gold they can later borrow against instead of selling. Gold pays you nothing while you hold it — that trade-off is the whole decision, and it is unpacked in why people buy gold below.

title: Buying gold
heading: What you actually own afterwards
text: You own Tether Gold , held in a self-custody vault whose address you can view in your profile. On Arbitrum the token is XAUt0 — contract 0x40461291347e1eCbb09499F3371D3f17f10d7159 — the cross-chain version of native XAUt. Each XAUt0 is backed 1:1 by native XAUt locked in an adapter contract on Ethereum, and each of those by one troy ounce of vaulted physical gold. The app labels the unit "XAUT" throughout; on Arbitrum the asset is precisely XAUt0. Fractional ownership is real, not notional. XAUt0 carries six decimals, so the smallest amount you can own is 0.000001 oz — about 0.0000311 g, or four-tenths of a cent at US$4,376/oz. There is no rounding up to a bar, no minimum weight, no queue to be allocated. A US$20 purchase gives you 0.004548 oz, yours the moment the transaction confirms. The physical backing sits in Swiss vaults. Auri's reserves screen names Brink's, Switzerland as custodian with serial-numbered bars, cites attestation by BDO Italia , and links to Tether Gold's own published data so you can check the figures against the issuer rather than against Auri. The legal structure — whether bars are titled in your name, held in bailment, or held by the issuer against your token — is UNKNOWN , and is the most important thing to settle on the trust page before committing meaningful money. You are not holding metal, and that means counterparties. Gold in your own safe has none. This has several: Tether Gold as issuer, the custodian holding the bars, the adapter contract holding the native XAUt, the Arbitrum network, and Auri as the interface. Any honest case for tokenised gold starts by admitting that stack exists. title: Buying gold
heading: Why people buy gold, and what it actually does
text: Gold has no cash flow. No dividend, no interest, no earnings. A business and a rental property pay you for waiting; gold pays you nothing and costs something to keep. Every argument for owning it has to survive that sentence first. The ones that do are narrow: Currency exposure, not returns. If all your savings sit in one national currency you are making a concentrated bet on that currency's purchasing power, whether you meant to or not. Gold holds part of your savings outside that bet. This is the strongest case, and it is about what you are exposed to rather than about going up. No issuer can print more of it. Supply grows slowly and by physical effort. That is the whole debasement argument — a decades-long thesis, not a this-quarter one. It moves differently from equities. Not reliably opposite — sometimes it falls alongside everything else — but differently enough that a modest allocation changes a portfolio's shape. What we will not tell you is how much to hold. Anyone naming a percentage without knowing your income, debts, timeline and temperament is selling, not advising. How this differs from an ETF or a price-tracking token An ETF share is a claim on a fund: bought through a broker, tradable only in market hours, charged an annual expense ratio, and in almost all cases not redeemable for metal by an ordinary holder. For pure price exposure inside a brokerage or tax-advantaged account it is often the cheaper answer, with familiar tax reporting and no on-chain mechanics to learn. What Auri gives instead: the holding sits in a vault you control, moves 24/7 including weekends, can be sent to a person rather than a broker, and can back a loan without being sold or credit-checked. title: Buying gold
heading: Buy it all at once, or spread it out?
text: Buying in one go: if you have decided you want the exposure, every day you are not holding is a day you remain fully exposed to the currency you were trying to diversify away from. Historically, investing immediately has more often beaten phasing in, because waiting means sitting in cash while prices drift upward. Spreading it out: this is a behavioural tool, and behaviour is where most people lose money. It removes the chance of putting your whole position in on the worst day of the year — the outcome that makes people abandon a plan entirely — and turns an intimidating one-off decision into a habit funded from income. Auto-Invest automates it from US$10 per cycle, daily, weekly or monthly, and tracks your average cost per ounce. Be clear what it does not do: it does not guarantee a profit and does not protect you in a sustained decline. If gold falls for three years, buying weekly for three years means losing money weekly. The honest framing is regret-minimisation, not risk-elimination. Fees do not settle the argument either way. Because the 0.49% is proportional rather than flat, twenty US$50 buys cost the same percentage as one US$1,000 buy — frequency is free. So cadence barely matters and sustainability matters enormously. Pick an amount you will not resent in month seven. When not to buy You need the money inside a year. Gold can fall 20% and stay there. Money with a deadline does not belong in a volatile asset, and a round trip costs about 1% before the price does anything. You are carrying high-interest debt. Paying down a 20% credit card is a guaranteed 20% return. No gold thesis beats that. You are buying because the price just jumped. title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Adding and withdrawing cash
text: Your cash balance is the dollar side of your Auri account — what you buy gold with, repay a loan with, and pull back out to your bank. This page covers every rail in and out, what each costs, how long it takes, and what you actually hold while the money sits there.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Why people keep a cash balance
text: Three reasons. A buy funded from cash is the fastest route into gold, because it skips the funding leg entirely. Repayments and collateral unlocks on a loan are paid out of cash. And Auto-Invest can auto-debit it on schedule. If you only make one-off bank-funded buys, you can ignore cash completely.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: What a cash balance actually is
text: It is not dollars in a bank account with your name on it. Your local currency is received on regulated payment rails, converted, and held as USDC — a US-dollar stablecoin — on Arbitrum, ready to buy gold or repay a loan. The asset is native USDC on Arbitrum One, contract 0xaf88d065e77c8cC2239327C5EDb3A432268e5831 , the same dollar you borrow against your gold. Not a deposit, not insured. Auri is not a bank. Deposit-insurance and investor-protection schemes cover bank deposits and brokerage accounts, not stablecoins: CDIC and CIPF in Canada, FDIC, NCUA and SIPC in the US, and equivalents elsewhere, do not apply here. They are named to show what does not cover you. A stablecoin targets one dollar; it does not guarantee one. USDC is an obligation of its issuer, redeemable on that issuer's terms. The peg is backed by reserves, not by a government. Your display currency is not what you hold. Auri offers 28 display currencies, but that setting only changes the number on screen. The unit underneath is US-dollar-referenced, so a balance shown in Canadian dollars, rupees or pounds moves whenever that currency moves against the dollar — including on days you do nothing. Cash carries currency risk if you do not think in US dollars, issuer risk no insurance absorbs, and it pays you nothing — no interest accrues on cash anywhere in the app. It is a staging area, not a savings account. One honest ambiguity: the app calls your gold vault self-custody and shows its address, while a sell receipt labels the matching cash credit as an internal USDC ledger entry. Whether cash sits in a wallet you control is UNKNOWN . See proof and custody .

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Before you start
text: An Auri account — see getting started . Interac, bank or debit: a one-time identity check. Method rows are tagged "ID required" or "ID verified" before you pick. Bank and Interac withdrawals: a destination account in your own name. USDC either way: a wallet that supports Arbitrum. The check fires only on a buy, add-cash or withdrawal using Interac, a bank or a debit card, and only the first time: legal name and date of birth, a photo of your licence or passport, then a selfie. Usually instant, and it returns you to the screen you came from. In Canada the app cites FINTRAC rules; the equivalent elsewhere is UNKNOWN .

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Add cash from Interac, a bank or a card
text: About a minute · no fee on Interac and bank deposits, 1% on debit · no cancel step once you confirm. Open Add cash. On the Actions tab, in the Cash group, or from the move-money menu on Home. Enter the amount. Currency only — no gram or ounce units here, unlike a gold buy. Chips add +$10, +$50, +$100 and +$500. Choose a deposit method. Interac e-Transfer, Bank account, Debit card, or Deposit USDC from a wallet. Clear the identity check if prompted. You return to the same flow when it completes. Read the review screen. Four lines: You add , Method , Held as USDC , Available — instant for Interac and debit, 1–2 hours for a bank transfer. People skim "Held as USDC"; it is telling you what you will own. Confirm. Processing tracks each leg live — receiving funds, converting to USDC, updating your balance, plus awaiting-bank-settlement for transfers. Minimise it and the job keeps running, then notifies you. Check the "Held as USDC" and "Available" lines before confirming. What you'll see when it works. A success screen, an updated balance on Home, and a row in Activity under the Cash filter — expand it for each leg with its reference or transaction hash.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Deposit USDC from your own wallet
text: This path works differently: instead of a review screen, the button becomes Deposit and Auri shows a deposit address labelled for USDC on Arbitrum, with a copy button. No identity check, no Auri fee, no quoted arrival time — the balance updates when the transfer confirms, and the network fee comes from the sending wallet. Send only USDC, only on Arbitrum . Other tokens or networks sent to that address may be lost, and blockchain transfers cannot be reversed. Send a small test amount the first time. Whether a wrong-network send can be recovered is UNKNOWN — assume not.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Withdraw cash
text: Under a minute to submit · CA$1.50 on Interac, no fee stated on bank transfer · irreversible once sent. Open Withdraw cash. From the Cash group on Actions , or the move-money menu. Enter the amount. Chips add +$10, +$50 and +$100; Max fills your whole balance. Cash is never locked as collateral — only gold is — so the full balance stays withdrawable even with a loan open. Pick a destination. Bank account (1–2 business days), Interac e-Transfer (instant, CA$1.50), or Crypto wallet, which reveals an address field. Clear the identity check if prompted. Bank and Interac rails only. Approve the step-up if you are sending to a wallet. A passkey, or two 6-digit codes — one emailed, one from your authenticator app. Auri cannot approve this step for you. Read the review screen. You withdraw , To , Arrives — 1–2 days for a bank transfer, instant for Interac, minutes for a wallet. Confirm. Processing shows redeeming USDC, converting to your currency, sending to your bank. The Activity receipt keeps the same breakdown. Bank and Interac withdrawals can only go to an account in your own name — third-party payouts are not permitted, so a withdrawal cannot be used to pay someone else. A USDC withdrawal goes out on Arbitrum and cannot be reversed; check the address character by character.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: Timing, and what happens underneath
text: Deposit rail depends on your country Cash balance a stablecoin balance, not a deposit Buy or repay or withdraw again Withdraw back to your own bank Your money becomes USDC at the second step and stays USDC until you withdraw — buying gold and repaying a loan never touch the banking rails again, which is why they are fast and a withdrawal is not. Every fiat leg settles on a schedule Auri does not control; every on-chain leg is fast. That asymmetry explains all the timings above. One inconsistency to know: add-cash quotes 1–2 hours for a bank transfer, while paying for gold straight from a bank transfer quotes 1–2 business days — plan around the longer figure and trust the number on your own review screen. Weekend and holiday cut-offs are UNKNOWN . Auri's rewards catalogue includes a fee-waiver reward covering one withdrawal, shown as worth CA$12.

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: When a cash balance makes sense — and when it doesn't
text: It makes sense when cash is a tool, not a destination. If you buy on a schedule, funding Auto-Invest from cash means a failed bank debit never skips a cycle. If a loan is open, a buffer lets you repay or unlock collateral the same day rather than waiting on a transfer — the unlock flow pays the matching part of the loan from cash, and shows a shortfall if the money is not there. It stops making sense when cash becomes the destination. Hold a balance for months and you hold a stablecoin with no interest, no insurance and — unless you think in US dollars — an exchange-rate exposure you did not choose. Money you need in a bank account soon belongs in a bank account: the round trip costs a rail fee each way plus one to two business days at the bank end. Two mistakes in particular: funding cash with money earmarked for a bill due this week, since the deposit is instant but the exit is not; and treating a balance as a repayment plan, when the consequences of an unpaid loan land on your gold — see liquidation and the risk page .

title: Adding and withdrawing cash
heading: What can go wrong
text: "My deposit says pending." Bank transfers carry an awaiting-settlement step. Expand the row in Activity to see which leg is outstanding. "I sent USDC and nothing arrived." Almost always the wrong network or token. The address accepts USDC on Arbitrum only; recovery is UNKNOWN . "My withdrawal was rejected over the account name." Payouts must go to an account in your own name. Withdraw to your own account, then pay the other person from there. "Why ID for a card deposit but not a USDC transfer?" Expected — the check is tied to fiat rails, not to the amount. "The app wants two codes." The step-up on an external-wallet withdrawal: the emailed code and your authenticator code, or a passkey instead.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Gifting, sending and remitting
text: Gold you own can leave your account three ways: as a gift the recipient claims through a link or QR code, as a send straight to another Auri user or an Arbitrum wallet, or — once it ships — as a cross-border remittance paid out in local currency. This page covers what each does, what the person on the other end has to do, and when not to use any of them.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Gift or send: which one you want
text: All of them move the same asset and all require step-up verification. What differs is who the recipient is and what they must do next. Use When What the recipient does Gift They probably have no Auri account, and you want an occasion, a message and something shareable. Opens a claim link or scans a QR code, creates an account, and the gold lands in their vault. Send to @username They already use Auri. Nothing. It arrives as gold, no claim link. Send to a wallet They self-custody and want the token itself. Nothing, but they must control an Arbitrum One wallet. Cannot be reversed. Remit They need spendable local currency, not gold. Nothing — payout lands in their account. Not live yet.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Before you start
text: You need gold already. These flows move gold you hold; they do not buy it. See Buy gold — funding is regional (Interac e-Transfer in Canada, bank transfer in the US). Only free gold can move. With a loan open, part of your gold is locked as collateral and cannot be gifted, sent or sold. The app caps the amount at your free balance; to move more, repay or unlock (see Borrow against gold ). Step-up verification is mandatory on every gift, send and remittance — a passkey approval, or two six-digit codes (one emailed, one from your authenticator). This is separate from signing in. For an @username send, get the handle exactly right — 3–20 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and underscores, set by the recipient in Profile. For a wallet send, get the address from the recipient directly. Never from a message you did not expect.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Gift gold
text: Time: about a minute. Cost: network fee covered by Auri; see fees and limits . Reversibility: cancellable any time before the recipient claims. Open Gift gold from the Actions catalogue or the move-money menu, under Move gold . Choose delivery. Contact sends the claim link for you, by mobile number or email — the mobile field offers dial codes for Canada, the US, India, the UK, the UAE, Singapore, Australia, the Philippines, Pakistan, Nigeria, Germany and France. Share link and QR code hand the claim back to you, so you can deliver it in a card, over a messaging app, or on a screen in person. Enter the amount in dollars, grams, ounces or XAUT, with the live equivalent shown in the other units. Presets are $50 / $100 / $250 / $500, or 1 / 5 / 10 / 25 g, or 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 oz. Capped at your free gold. Pick an occasion — Birthday, Wedding, Festival, Shagun, Congrats, or Just because. This is presentation, not mechanics: it changes what the recipient sees on opening the claim. Add a message. Optional, and the part people actually remember. Complete step-up verification. Check the review screen: gift value, the amount in gold (oz), delivery method, occasion. The gold figure is the one that matters — that is what the recipient ends up owning, whatever the price does later. Confirm. The gold moves into gift escrow on Arbitrum and a claim link is generated. Contact gifts confirm the link is on its way; link and QR gifts show the claim URL with Copy, WhatsApp and Email share. The review screen is the last place to check the gold amount before the gift enters escrow. What you'll see when it works A success screen naming the amount in ounces, plus the claim URL for link and QR gifts. The gift then appears in Activity with a Pending claim badge, and Home shows a banner counti

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: How the recipient claims
text: They open the link or scan the QR, create an Auri account if needed, and the gold moves from escrow into their vault. From then it is theirs: hold, sell, send onward, borrow against, or move to their own wallet. You cannot take it back. Tell the recipient it is coming before you send it. An unannounced message containing a gold claim link looks exactly like a scam, and that is the most common reason gifts sit unclaimed. Claiming means signing up: passwordless sign-in, and biometrics on mobile. Auri's identity check is triggered by funding and cash-out rails — bank transfer, debit card, Interac — so claiming a gift and holding the gold does not by itself require ID. The moment they want to sell and withdraw cash, it will.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Unclaimed gifts, reminders and cancelling
text: Until claimed, the gold sits in escrow: out of your spendable balance, not yet the recipient's. In Activity, a pending gift states that the recipient has not claimed it and that the gold stays on hold until they do. Two actions sit on that row: Remind / re-send — re-delivers the claim to the same contact. Cancel gift — pulls the gold out of escrow back to your free balance, confirmed as the gift cancelled and funds returned. You choose amount plus an occasion Link, QR or contact sent to the recipient They claim sign in and accept They own gold an asset, not a voucher Unclaimed gifts stay yours until the recipient accepts. A gift is not the recipient's until they claim it — until then it is escrowed and you can still pull it back. Auri's V2.2 prototype states no expiry period for an unclaimed gift and no automatic refund after a set number of days. Until that is published, treat an unclaimed gift as something you must chase or cancel yourself. Escrowed value still tracks the gold price while it waits — it is not parked in dollars.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Send gold to a person or a wallet
text: Time: immediate to an @username . Cost: network fee covered; see fees and limits . Reversibility: a wallet send is irreversible on confirmation. Open Send gold and choose Contact , @Username , or Wallet . Enter the destination. Contact takes a mobile number (same dial-code picker) or an email. @Username delivers as gold immediately with no claim step. Wallet takes an Arbitrum address and shows an irreversibility warning worth reading. Enter the amount in dollars, grams, ounces or XAUT. Presets $50 / $100 / $250 / $500, capped at your free gold. Complete step-up verification. Check the review screen: amount, gold equivalent, destination, and method — On-chain wallet or Claim as gold . If it says Claim as gold , the recipient must claim it exactly like a gift. Confirm. A wallet send cannot be undone, and Auri cannot recover it. The asset that arrives is XAUt0 on Arbitrum One — the LayerZero version of Tether Gold, contract 0x40461291347e1eCbb09499F3371D3f17f10d7159 . The receiving wallet must support Arbitrum One and be able to display that token, or the balance looks missing even though the transfer succeeded. Send a small test amount to any new address first. A typo, the wrong network, or an exchange deposit address that does not accept XAUt0 all mean the gold is gone.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Cross-border remittance
text: Coming soon — you cannot do this today. Remittance is modelled in Auri's V2.2 prototype but is not in the live product. What follows describes the intended flow; do not plan a real payment around it. The design converts gold or your cash balance into a local-currency payout: pick a destination country, choose to fund from gold or cash, enter an amount, and a live panel shows what the recipient receives, the rate, the fee and an expected arrival time. Then payout details, step-up verification, review, and a processing state. The stated fee is 0.7% of the amount sent, with mid-market rates and no FX markup claimed — that second part is the substantive one, because remittance cost normally hides in the FX margin, not the visible fee. For scale, the World Bank puts the global average cost of sending $200 at 6.49% in Q1 2025 (banks 9.50%, digital providers 3.65%). Judge any number all-in. Corridor Payout methods Details required India (INR) UPI, or bank account UPI ID, or account number + IFSC code Philippines (PHP) Bank account, or GCash Account number + bank name, or GCash number Mexico (MXN) Bank (CLABE) 18-digit CLABE United States (USD) Bank account Account number + routing number United Kingdom (GBP) Bank account Sort code + account number The receipt breaks the transfer into auditable legs: gold sold to USDC on Uniswap v3, USDC converted to local currency, then payout over local rails. So funding from gold means selling gold — you give up the exposure, and the disposal has tax consequences. Remittance is also the one flow that always passes through a processing state, because a real bank with real cut-offs sits on the other side: a transfer started late on a Friday can land after the weekend however fast the on-chain legs are.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Why gift gold instead of a gift card
text: A gift card is a liability of a merchant: dollar-denominated, usable in one place, quietly eroded by inflation, and frequently never fully spent. A gold gift is different in kind — the recipient owns a claim on a specific quantity of vaulted metal, sellable anywhere Auri operates, with a price unrelated to any company's solvency. Five grams is five grams in ten years. Five grams is not a promise from a retailer. The unit matters more than people expect. Grams read as a gift; dollars read as a transfer. "Ten grams for your wedding" is an object; a dollar figure is a bank notification. That is why you can type the amount in grams or ounces directly, and why a round weight usually lands better than a round price. Occasions where it works The built-in occasions track where gold gifting is already a norm rather than a novelty: weddings, births, milestone birthdays, and festival gifting — Shagun and Diwali in South Asian households, where giving gold at an auspicious time is the tradition itself. It also suits the graduation or first-job gift where you specifically do not want the money spent this month. Gold is illiquid in the useful sense: claiming is easy, spending takes a deliberate decision. What the recipient is taking on Be honest that you are signing someone up for an app. If they ever want cash rather than gold, they will go through an identity check and a bank connection. For a confident adult that is a short errand; for an older relative it may be a phone call with you walking them through it — budget for that call, or hand over the QR code in person and do it together. Set price expectations too: gold pays no dividend and no interest, it has had long stretches of falling real value, and a gift given at a high price can be worth less a year later. If a fixed sum on

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: Tax and reporting
text: Giving gold away is still a disposal of an asset in many tax systems, even though no cash reached you. Depending on where you live, a gift can trigger a capital gain measured from what you paid to the value on the day you gave it; some countries tax or require reporting of gifts above a threshold, on the giver's side, the recipient's side, or both; and treatment differs again for gifts to a spouse, to a minor, or across a border. Funding a remittance from gold is unambiguously a sale. Profile includes a Tax & reports section with transaction-history export and realised gain/loss figures — the raw material an accountant will ask for. The obligation is yours. Thresholds and treatment vary by country and change; check your own jurisdiction and get a qualified adviser if a gift is large.

title: Gifting, sending and remitting
heading: What can go wrong
text: The recipient hasn't claimed the gift Open Activity, find the row badged Pending claim , then use Remind / re-send or Cancel gift to return the gold. Message the person yourself first — most unclaimed gifts are unclaimed because the link looked untrustworthy. Only part of my gold is free to move You have a loan open and the rest is locked as collateral. Repay, or unlock a specific amount of collateral, then retry. See Borrow against gold . I sent gold to the wrong wallet address There is no recovery — Auri cannot reverse an on-chain transfer and neither can anyone else. If the address belongs to an exchange or a wallet you can contact, that is your only avenue and it usually fails. Hence the small test transfer to any new address. The @username wasn't found Handles are 3–20 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and underscores, and the recipient must have set one in Profile. Confirm the spelling, or send to their mobile number or email and let them claim. I can't find remittance in the app It is not released. title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: Auto-invest (DCA)
text: An Auto-Invest plan is a standing instruction: Auri buys a fixed amount of money's worth of gold every day, week or month at whatever the live price is at that moment, and reports the whole plan back to you as a single average cost per ounce. It takes about a minute to set up, there is no setup fee, and you can pause, resize or stop it whenever you want.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: Why people do this
text: Buying gold in one go means making one price decision, and most people make that decision badly — they buy after a rally and stop after a fall. A recurring plan removes the decision: the money is fixed, the timing is fixed, and only the number of ounces you receive varies. It is a budgeting and behaviour tool first and a pricing tool second. Read About dollar-cost averaging below before you commit to a monthly amount.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: Before you start
text: An Auri account. See Start here . At least $10 per cycle. The app rejects anything smaller with "Enter at least $10 per cycle" . A funding source you can sustain for months, not weeks: your cash balance, a linked bank account, or a per-cycle top-up reminder. If you fund from a bank account, the one-time identity check has to be complete first — bank rails require it, and crypto funding does not. See Start here . An understanding that gold pays no interest, no dividend and no rent. A plan accumulates metal, not income. About 1 minute to set up · 0.49% Auri fee on each buy, setup fee free, network fee covered · each individual buy is irreversible once it executes, but the plan itself is cancellable at any time.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: Create a recurring plan
text: Open Auto-Invest. Reach it from the main navigation, from the Auto-Invest card on Home, or from the Actions catalogue. The page opens on your existing plans with an inline form for a new one. Enter the amount per cycle. Minimum $10. This is an amount of money , not an amount of gold — that is the entire mechanic. When gold is expensive the same $200 buys fewer ounces; when it is cheap it buys more. Choose the frequency. Daily , Weekly or Monthly . That is the complete list — there is no payday option and no custom interval. The schedule anchors to the moment you start the plan, so if you start a weekly plan on the day you get paid, every later buy lands on that same weekday. Pick where the money comes from. Three options: Cash balance (auto-debited from your USDC cash each cycle — the most reliable, because nothing external has to succeed); Bank account (auto-debited each cycle over local bank rails — EFT in Canada, bank transfer in the US); or a top-up reminder , where Auri does not pull anything and instead reminds you each cycle to fund the buy yourself (in Canada that top-up is Interac e-Transfer). The reminder option is the only one that will not execute on its own. Check the review screen. It shows Each investment , Frequency , In gold (an approximate ounce figure at the current price), Funded from , and Setup fee: Free . The ounce figure is an estimate at today's price, not a commitment — the actual ounces are set by the live price at each execution. Confirm. The plan starts immediately with its first buy. Confirmation reads "Auto-Invest started — Auri will buy $X of gold weekly, starting now. Manage, pause or stop it anytime."

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: What you'll see when it works
text: Each plan appears as its own card showing the amount, the cadence, its status, the next buy and last buy dates, gold accumulated, invested to date, number of buys, average price paid, current worth, and return in both dollars and percent. The page header aggregates the same figures across every plan you run, including a blended average cost. The number to sanity-check after the second cycle is buys count . If it has not incremented on schedule, the plan did not execute — check the funding source before anything else. Gold bought by a plan is ordinary vault gold: it is free to sell, gift or send, and it earns 2× Auri Jewels instead of the standard 1 Jewel per $1 bought. Rates are on the reference page .

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: Pause, edit, resume and stop
text: Pause keeps the plan and its history intact and stops future buys. Nothing is sold. This is also how you skip a single cycle — there is no dedicated skip control, so you pause, let the date pass, and resume. Resume restarts the cadence from the moment you resume, not from where it left off. Edit changes the amount and the frequency in place. Your accumulated gold, buys count and average cost carry over, so a plan you resize keeps reporting one blended average across both the old and the new amount. If you want a clean before-and-after record, stop the plan and start a second one instead. Stop ends the plan permanently. It does not sell anything — the gold stays in your vault and simply stops growing. Set a plan amount plus cadence Runs on schedule daily, weekly or monthly Averages your cost buys at whatever the price is Pause anytime no fee to stop Stopping a plan never sells gold — only the buying stops. Pausing is the reversible version of the same thing. Coming soon. Scheduling and managing recurring buys from the Auri CLI, the REST API, or an AI agent over MCP is not live yet. Today, plans are created and managed in the app only.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: How a plan reports average cost and P&L
text: Average cost is straightforward arithmetic: total invested ÷ total ounces the plan has bought . Because each buy spends the same money at a different price, that average is not the simple average of the prices you paid — it is pulled below it, because a fixed amount buys more ounces at low prices than at high ones. Worked example, four weekly buys of $200. The prices are illustrative, not a forecast; your app uses the live price. Cycle Gold price (illustrative) You invest Gold received (after 0.49% fee) 1 $4,400/oz $200 0.0452 oz 2 $4,000/oz $200 0.0498 oz 3 $3,800/oz $200 0.0524 oz 4 $4,200/oz $200 0.0474 oz Plan total simple average $4,100/oz $800 0.1947 oz The plan reports an average cost of $4,108/oz — that is $800 ÷ 0.1947 oz. Strip the 0.49% fee out and the pure averaging effect got you gold at $4,088/oz against a simple price average of $4,100/oz. That $12 gap is the whole of what averaging bought you over four cycles. It is real, and it is small. Three things the reported return does not tell you: It is unrealised and pre-cost. Selling costs another 0.49%, and any tax consequence is yours. See fees and limits . The percentage is not comparable to a lump-sum return. Your first dollar has been invested for months and your most recent dollar for days. A plan showing "+7%" has not earned 7% on all of your money for the whole period. Average cost is not a floor. It is a record of what you paid. The price can and does sit below it for long stretches. Per-plan average cost, gold accumulated and buys count, with the aggregate blended average across all plans in the header.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: What a schedule costs over three years
text: Auri's buy fee is a flat percentage with no per-transaction minimum, so cadence barely affects cost. Roughly $3,600 a year, run three ways for three years: Plan Buys in 3 years Total invested Total Auri fee at 0.49% $10 daily 1,095 $10,950 $53.66 $70 weekly 156 $10,920 $53.51 $300 monthly 36 $10,800 $52.92 Thirty-six buys and 1,095 buys cost within a dollar of each other. Choose the cadence that matches your income, not the one you think is cheaper. Price impact is shown as under 0.1% and the network fee is covered, so those do not scale with buy count either.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: What can go wrong
text: "My plan didn't buy this week." Check the funding source on the plan card. A top-up reminder plan never executes on its own — it waits for you to fund it. "I set the minimum and it wouldn't save." The floor is $10 per cycle, checked before the review step. "My average cost went up after I edited the plan." Editing blends the new amount into the existing history rather than starting fresh. Stop and start a new plan if you need separate records. "I can't sell the gold my plan bought." If you have an open loan, some of your gold is locked as collateral and cannot be sold, gifted or sent until you repay or unlock it. Plan buys add to your total, and borrowing against that total locks it. See Borrow against gold . A failed bank collection. The app does not currently state what happens when a scheduled bank debit is declined — whether it retries, skips, or pauses the plan. Treat this as UNKNOWN and watch the buys count until it is documented.

title: Auto-invest (DCA)
heading: About dollar-cost averaging
text: What it does Dollar-cost averaging means investing equal amounts at regular intervals regardless of the price. Mechanically it does exactly two things. It makes your ounces-per-dollar vary inversely with price, so a fixed budget buys more when gold is cheap. And it takes the timing decision away from you, which for most people is the larger effect by a wide margin. What it does not do It does not guarantee a profit. It does not protect you against loss. In a sustained decline, a plan buys the whole way down and you end up holding more ounces at a lower price than you started with — averaging reduces how badly a single bad entry hurts, it does not remove the exposure. Anyone describing DCA as a risk-management technique is overselling it: it manages regret, not risk. Rising and falling markets, on identical numbers Four $200 buys, $800 total, against putting the whole $800 in on day one. Falling market — $4,400, $4,100, $3,800, $3,500. The plan accumulates 0.2030 oz at an average cost of $3,941/oz, worth $711 at the end: down $89, or 11% . The lump sum bought 0.1809 oz at $4,400, worth $633: down $167, or 21% . Averaging lost less. It still lost. Rising market — the same four prices in the opposite order: $3,800, $4,000, $4,200, $4,400. The plan accumulates 0.1947 oz at $4,108/oz, worth $857: up $57, or 7% . The lump sum bought 0.2095 oz at $3,800, worth $922: up $122, or 15% . Averaging earned less. That is the honest trade, and it is symmetric: spreading purchases in narrows the range of outcomes in both directions. Historically, investing a lump sum immediately has more often beaten spreading it in, because markets rise more often than they fall. People still choose to spread in, and reasonably so — a smaller worst case is worth paying for if the worst case is what wo

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Borrowing against your gold
text: A loan against your gold turns metal you already own into dollars you can spend, without selling an ounce. Your gold is pledged as collateral, USDC is borrowed against it and credited to your Auri cash balance, and your gold exposure stays exactly where it was — same ounces, same upside. There is no repayment schedule and no maturity date. The trade-off is real: you are borrowing against an asset whose price moves, and if it moves far enough against you, your gold gets sold to clear the debt.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: What actually happens when you borrow
text: Three things happen when you confirm, and only three: Your gold is pledged, not sold. The XAUt0 backing your balance becomes collateral. You pay no buy or sell spread and your ounce count does not change by a gram. USDC is borrowed against it and credited to your Auri cash balance as spendable cash. Interest starts accruing on the borrowed amount, continuously, at a rate that floats. The loan is not an Auri ledger entry. It is a position in a public lending market — a Morpho market on Arbitrum One pairing XAUt0 collateral with USDC loans. Open that link without an account and read its supply, borrowing, utilisation, live rate and liquidation parameter yourself. Auri is the interface; the credit lives on chain. Borrowing does not reduce your gold balance. It reduces how much of that gold you are allowed to move — see Locked gold cannot leave . Gold locked as collateral, not sold Morpho market XAUt0 collateral, USDC borrowed USDC to you spend, hold or withdraw Repay anytime no fixed schedule Your gold keeps its full upside while it is collateral. Your gold never moves when you borrow — only the stablecoin leg does.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Before you start
text: Gold in your account that is free — not already locked against a loan. If you have none, start at Buying gold . An amount in mind, and a plan for repaying it. Read why people borrow before picking the number. To move the cash to a bank, a one-time identity check. Borrowing alone needs no ID check, because no money leaves your account. No open Boost position — the two cannot coexist, and the app blocks whichever you open second. About a minute in the app · the review screen shows no Auri fee and no network fee, so your cost is floating interest · fully reversible by repaying, any time, in any amount. A liquidation is not reversible.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Borrow cash against your gold
text: Open the borrow flow. On the Actions tab, under Borrow , select Borrow cash . It is also on the home loan card and in the move-money menu. Set the amount. Drag the slider, tap a 10% / 25% / 50% / Max chip, or nudge with the ±$100 steppers. The field opens at roughly 30% of the maximum rather than at the maximum, deliberately. Read the live panel. Cash you receive, estimated monthly interest, your liquidation price, a now-to-after table for loan balance, loan-to-value and health factor, and a risk label for the amount chosen. Check the detail rows. Current loan, cash received as USDC, gold locked as collateral in ounces, new loan-to-value, the rate, liquidation price. If any of those surprises you, lower the amount. Review the summary. It restates what you borrow, your new loan-to-value, the rate, the liquidation price, your health factor after the draw, and that you receive it as Cash · USDC. Confirm. No step-up verification and no processing wait, because nothing leaves your account. You land on Cash borrowed — your gold stays intact , with the on-chain legs on the receipt. The review step is the one screen worth reading twice: loan-to-value, rate, liquidation price and health factor, all before you confirm.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: The four numbers that matter
text: Loan-to-value (LTV) — what you owe divided by the value of all the gold in your account, not just the slice labelled locked. Borrow US$10,000 against 10 oz worth US$40,000 and your LTV is 25%. Health factor — your distance from liquidation as one number. Bigger is safer; 1.0 means you are standing on the line. The app computes and colours it live; read it there rather than deriving it. Liquidation price — the gold price at which your LTV reaches the market's liquidation loan-to-value of 77%: what you owe ÷ (your ounces × 0.77). A US$10,000 loan against 10 oz liquidates near US$1,299/oz. Estimated interest — a projection at the current rate. Because the rate floats, it is an estimate, not a bill. One identity is worth memorising: gold can fall by (1 − your LTV ÷ 0.77) before you are liquidated. At 25% LTV that is a 67.5% fall. At 50% it is 35%. At 70% it is 9%.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: The rate floats, and interest never stops
text: Auri does not set the rate. The lending market produces it from how much of the available USDC is being borrowed: utilisation up, rate up, changing continuously — checks an hour apart have returned around 3.48% and 3.70%. The live number appears on the home page and in the app before you confirm. That is the figure to trust, not one printed in documentation. There is no monthly bill. Interest accrues into the balance you owe, which has a consequence people miss: your LTV drifts upward on its own, even if gold does nothing. A US$10,000 loan at 3.5% against US$40,000 of gold becomes about US$10,350 after a year, taking a 25.0% LTV to 25.9% with a flat price. You can also only draw what the market has available to lend at that moment, so a large borrow may need splitting or may not fill. A loan you never touch still grows. If you intend to leave a position open for years, check it quarterly and pay down interest occasionally rather than letting the balance compound against a fixed pile of collateral.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Getting the cash out — or leaving it in
text: Borrowed USDC lands in your cash balance and you do not have to withdraw it; leaving it there is often right, because it is the dry powder you will repay with. Rails are regional — bank transfer in the United States, Interac e-Transfer or bank EFT in Canada, or USDC to a wallet you control on Arbitrum. Two rules to plan around: bank and Interac payouts can only go to an account in your own name , and a first fiat withdrawal triggers the one-time identity check. Amounts, timings and fees are on Cash in and out . Coming soon. Spending borrowed cash on the Auri card, sending it abroad as a cross-border transfer, and drawing or repaying a loan through the API, CLI or MCP integration are not live. The card is currently a waitlist.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Repaying, and getting your gold back
text: Repayment has no schedule: any amount, any time, from your cash balance. There are three ways out, and it is worth knowing all three before you need one. Repay from cash. Open Repay loan and set an amount with the slider or 10% / 25% / 50% / Max chips — Max is capped by whichever is smaller, your loan or your cash. Remaining loan, health factor, LTV and liquidation price update as you drag, and the liquidation row reads Cleared once the loan is gone. Unlock collateral. Unlock is its own flow, not a cleanup step. Choose how much locked gold to free with the slider or 25% / 50% / 75% / All chips, and Auri repays the matching portion of the loan from your cash automatically. If your cash is short it states exactly how much more you need and hands you into Add cash . Sell free gold to repay. The last resort and the most expensive, because it crystallises the sale you were avoiding. Only free gold can be sold, so if everything is locked you must unlock first — which itself needs cash. A fourth route lowers risk without repaying anything: buy more gold . Adding collateral cuts your LTV and pushes your liquidation price down without needing dollars for a repayment.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Locked gold cannot leave
text: While a loan is open, Auri splits your gold into locked and free and shows both on the home card, the loan profile and inside every outbound flow. Free gold behaves normally; locked gold cannot be sold, gifted, sent or transferred out, and attempting it tells you only part of your holding is free to move while the rest backs your loan. Collateral is locked at the market's ratio, so roughly every US$1,000 borrowed locks about US$1,300 of gold. Note the asymmetry: the split governs what you may move , but your LTV, health factor and liquidation price are calculated against all your gold — which is why buying more gold improves your risk position even though it does not change your loan.

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Liquidation: how it works, and how to stay away from it
text: The market has a liquidation loan-to-value of 77% . When what you owe reaches 77% of what your collateral is worth, anyone in the world can repay part or all of your debt and take collateral in exchange, at a discount set by the market. It is automatic and permissionless. Nobody phones you, there is no grace period, and there is nothing to negotiate. Treat 77% as a wall, not a target. Two figures locate the wall: your liquidation gold price is what you owe ÷ (your ounces × 0.77), and your buffer is 1 − (your LTV ÷ 0.77), the fall gold can take from today before you hit it. The app shows your exact liquidation price, health factor and remaining buffer live, updating as the price moves and interest accrues. Those live figures are authoritative; the arithmetic here is so you can sanity-check them. Safe 20% Conservative 35% Balanced 55% Risky 77% gold sold at 77% Stay well left of the line; a falling gold price pushes you right. The gap between where you borrow and 77% is the only protection you have — and it shrinks from both ends. What a liquidation costs you Plainly: your gold is sold at the worst possible moment, in a falling market, because that is by definition when liquidations happen. You lose more gold than the debt was worth, because the liquidator takes collateral at a discount as their incentive. You keep the leftover collateral and the dollars you already spent, but the position you were preserving is gone. And unlike borrowing, a liquidation is a sale of your gold, so in many countries it is a taxable disposal — at the price you would least have chosen. What causes one, and what prevents it Gold falls. The obvious cause, and the one people plan for. Interest accrues. The slow one — your LTV rises with the price perfectly flat. You borrowed near the ceiling. Th

title: Borrowing against your gold
heading: Why people borrow instead of selling — and when they shouldn't
text: The mechanics above tell you how. This is about whether. Borrowing against gold has a narrow set of good uses, and the difference is almost always about repayment rather than about gold. Borrow or sell? Your situation Borrowing Selling You want to keep the gold exposure Keeps it entirely Ends it Cost Floating interest for as long as you owe 0.49% Auri fee on the sale, and again if you buy back Tax treatment Generally not a disposal Generally a disposal, which can crystallise a gain Risk added Liquidation risk if gold falls far enough None — the position is closed Ongoing attention Yes, indefinitely No Reversible Yes, by repaying Only by buying back at whatever the price then is If you no longer want the gold exposure, sell. Borrowing to avoid admitting you want out is the worst version of this product. Liquidity without a disposal This is why most people are here. Selling gold held for years can crystallise a gain and a tax bill in the year you sell; borrowing against it generally does not, because you have disposed of nothing and still own the same ounces. That is general information about how borrowing differs from selling, not tax advice — treatment varies by country and by your circumstances, and rules change, so confirm with a qualified adviser before treating a tax outcome as a reason to borrow. Note the sting: a liquidation is a sale, so borrowing to avoid a disposal can force the very disposal you were avoiding. Bridging a cash gap The cleanest use. A payment falls due before money you already expect arrives — a contract payment, a refund, a property completion. The loan lives for weeks, the repayment source is identified, and the cost is small because the duration is short: US$10,000 for two months at 3.5% is roughly US$58. title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Repaying and unlocking gold
text: Repaying improves every number on your position at once: the balance owed falls, your loan-to-value falls, your liquidation price moves further away, and gold that was locked as collateral becomes free to sell, send or gift. There is no schedule and no due date — you choose when, and how much.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Why people repay
text: Three reasons cover almost all of it: you want your gold back in a spendable state, you want more distance between today's gold price and your liquidation price, or you are done with the loan and want to stop paying interest. Repaying is a risk dial, not a discipline exercise — see Repay early, or let it ride? for how to size it.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Before you start
text: An open loan. Loan profile shows your balance owed, LTV, liquidation price and collateral split. Cash in your Auri balance. Repayment comes from cash (USDC), never from gold. If you have none, add cash or sell free gold — locked collateral cannot be sold. Nothing else: no extra verification, no waiting period, no minimum term. About a minute · no Auri fee shown on the repay or unlock review screen, network fees covered · effective immediately, and you can re-borrow later at the rate in force then. Repaying and unlocking move nothing out of your account, so neither triggers the step-up authentication that gift, send, remit and external-wallet withdrawals require, and neither has a processing delay.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Repay part or all of your loan
text: Open Repay. On the Home loan card, on Loan profile , or in Actions as "Repay loan · Lower your LTV". Choose an amount. The sheet is headed Repay from cash with your available cash beside it. Use the slider or the 10% / 25% / 50% / Max chips. Max is the smaller of your loan and your cash, so it does not always clear the loan. Read the now → after rows. Remaining loan, health factor, new LTV and liquidation price update live. Clear the loan entirely and the liquidation price row reads Cleared . Check the review screen. It restates the repayment, that it comes from Cash · USDC, and your remaining loan, new LTV and new liquidation price. That screen is the authority on your numbers, not this page. Confirm. Success reads "Loan repaid — your loan-to-value is lower and more gold is freed up." What you'll see when it works: cash down by the repayment, loan down by the same amount, free gold up by roughly US$1.30 of gold per US$1 repaid. The transaction lands in Activity under the Borrow filter and expands into its on-chain legs with hashes you can open on Arbiscan.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: What repaying actually changes
text: Your gold does not move when you repay, and it did not move when you borrowed. Only the debt against the same metal changes, and three figures follow from that ratio. Loan-to-value is the balance owed divided by your collateral's market value, so repaying shrinks the numerator and LTV falls at once. Auri labels portfolio LTV Safe to 30%, Balanced to 55%, At risk above. Liquidation price is the gold price at which the position is closed out; less debt means a lower one, which the app also states as "your gold can fall X% before liquidation". Health factor is the app's summary figure — its liquidation threshold divided by your LTV, labelled safe above 1.0, green from 2.0, amber below 1.3. Read it in the app rather than computing it, and note the underlying Morpho market's liquidation loan-to-value is 77% : a level to stay well clear of. See how liquidation works . A worked example Illustrative round numbers. You hold 3.000 oz with gold at US$4,000/oz — US$12,000 of collateral — and have borrowed US$4,000.   Before After repaying US$1,000 Balance owed US$4,000 US$3,000 Loan-to-value 33.3% 25.0% Liquidation price at a 77% threshold ≈US$1,731/oz ≈US$1,298/oz Gold can fall ≈57% ≈68% Gold locked as collateral 1.299 oz 0.974 oz Gold free to move 1.701 oz 2.026 oz US$1,000 bought 0.325 oz of freedom and pushed the liquidation price down US$433/oz. The benefit is not linear: the first slice of a large loan moves that price a long way, the last slice of a small one barely moves it. Repay some loan falls Your share drops you owe less against the same gold Buffer widens gold can fall further before a sale Unlock gold collateral freed Repaying does not move your gold — it moves the price at which you would be liquidated further below today's price.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Locked gold and free gold
text: Borrowing reclassifies part of your holding. Auri splits gold into locked (backing the loan) and free , shown on the Home gold card, in the Loan profile collateral breakdown — total, locked, free, in ounces and your display currency — and inside every outbound flow. Locked gold is not spendable. Sell, gift, send or remit more than your free balance and the flow blocks: "Only $X (Y oz) is free to move. The rest is locked as collateral for your loan — repay to unlock it."

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Unlock collateral back to freely-transferable gold
text: Unlock is not a cleanup step after repaying — it is the same lever pulled from the other end. You choose an amount of gold to free and Auri repays the matching slice of the loan from your cash automatically. That slice is 77% of the freed gold's value, because 77% is the ratio it was locked at. Open Unlock gold. From Actions or Loan profile. Choose how much locked gold to free. Slider from zero to your total locked collateral, with 25% / 50% / 75% / All chips. Read the cash cost. Auri shows the loan portion it must repay — freed gold value × 0.77 — with a now → after table for LTV and health factor. Fund it if you are short. If cash does not cover it the sheet turns red — "You need $X more cash to repay the matching loan. Add cash to continue." — and Continue stays disabled, with an inline hand-off to Add cash . Review and confirm. The review lists gold freed, loan repaid from cash, cash after, new liquidation price and remaining loan. Use repay when you have a cash figure in mind; use unlock when you have a gold figure in mind — 0.5 oz to send to family, say. Both produce identical positions. One genuine trap: unlocking requires cash, and raising cash by selling requires free gold. Near the top of your borrowing capacity you have very little free gold, so the only route out may be adding cash from outside. Keep a cash buffer if you run a high LTV. Repaying via agent, CLI or API is not available yet. Every repayment today is one you initiate in the app — nothing pays your loan down for you, and there is no auto-deleverage setting.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Nothing is scheduled, but interest still accrues
text: No monthly payment, no due date, no minimum instalment. The consequence: interest is added to the balance you owe rather than billed separately. The Loan profile ledger breaks it out — principal borrowed, received as cash, gold locked, interest accrued, current balance owed — and that last figure is what your LTV and liquidation price are computed from. So a loan you never touch gets slightly riskier every day even if gold does not move. At a rate near 3.5% the debt grows about 3.5% a year, so your liquidation price climbs about 3.5% a year on its own. Above, US$4,000 owed becomes roughly US$4,140 after a silent year, LTV drifts to 34.5%, and the liquidation price rises to about US$1,792/oz. The rate floats — set by supply and demand in the underlying Morpho market, not fixed by Auri. In checks an hour apart it moved from roughly 3.48% to 3.70%. Never plan on a fixed cost of carry; the live figure in the app is the only one that counts, and anyone can inspect the market ( Trust and proof ).

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Repay early, or let it ride?
text: You are comparing one number you know against one you do not. The carry is knowable: near 3.5%, a US$4,000 loan costs about US$11.70 a month, roughly US$140 a year. What gold does next is not, and nothing here should be read as a view on it. Carry versus the cost of just selling Selling has its own cost. Auri charges 0.49% on a sell and 0.49% again on the buy-back, so a round trip is about 0.98% — US$39 on US$4,000 — plus any tax consequence and the risk of buying back higher. At US$11.70 a month the loan is cheaper for a little over three months and dearer after that. Short timing gaps favour borrowing; open-ended needs favour selling. Paying down before a period you cannot watch Not because volatility is predictable, but because your buffer is asymmetric: a fall in gold raises your LTV at exactly the moment your collateral is worth less and your free gold raises less cash. Repaying costs the same on a quiet Tuesday as in a panic — but on the quiet Tuesday you also choose the amount. Sizing it Target a percentage, not a payment. Decide the LTV you want to sit at, then repay to it. Auri's bands are a starting frame, not advice. Price your comfort in percent-fall terms. "Gold can fall 57%" is a better decision input than "33% LTV". Pay the first slice first. The liquidation price moves most per dollar at high LTV, so partial repayments are worth most exactly when you least want to make them. Do not use a projected return to justify carrying debt. The app's Auto-Invest projection hard-codes an 8.5%/yr assumption for illustration — an assumption, not a forecast. See Risks . Letting it ride is legitimate. At a low LTV, with cash on hand and a reason you still want the exposure, carrying the loan is the point of borrowing rather than selling. What makes that defensible is th

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: When not to repay, and when not to unlock
text: Not with money you need within weeks. Cash spent repaying may have to be re-borrowed, and not at the rate you repaid at. Not down to zero cash. Your cash buffer is what lets you respond to a fall in gold; at high LTV, a lower LTV bought with the whole buffer is a net downgrade. Do not unlock gold you have no plan for. Unlocking costs cash and only makes gold movable. If you are not selling, sending or gifting it, a plain repayment does the same risk work. Do not unlock to sell into a falling market without noticing you pay 0.49% and crystallise the loss. Repaying cuts the same risk without a sale.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: What can go wrong
text: "Max" doesn't clear my loan. The cap is the lower of your loan and your cash. Add cash, or sell free gold, then repay again. My health factor barely moved. Expected at low LTV — the relationship is not linear. Check the liquidation price instead. My LTV rose and I didn't borrow. Gold fell, or accrued interest grew the balance owed. The ledger separates principal from interest. I can't sell or send my gold. It is locked as collateral. Repay or unlock first; the flow states how much is free. Unlock is greyed out. You are short of the cash needed to repay 77% of the freed gold's value. I can't open a Boost position. A standard loan and a Boost position cannot both be open; repay the standard loan in full first. On Boost , reducing a position uses partial close (25/50/75/100%), not this flow.

title: Repaying and unlocking gold
heading: Related and next steps
text: Turn on the loan-health alert — it reports both your LTV and the current liquidation price. Then read how liquidation works properly, so the numbers here mean something. Borrowing against your gold covers sizing the next loan; fees and limits live in one place, Reference . Auri does not provide financial, tax or legal advice. Borrowing against gold can lead to the forced sale of your collateral. Figures here are illustrative; the live gold price, the live borrow rate and your own position numbers are shown in the app and are the only authoritative ones.

title: Boost — leverage
heading: Boost — leverage
text: Boost borrows US dollars against gold you already own, buys more gold with them, and pledges that gold too — looping until your exposure reaches the multiplier you picked. It multiplies gains and losses by the same factor, and adds a failure mode plain gold holding does not have: forced closure.

title: Boost — leverage
heading: What Boost actually is
text: The app's How leverage works panel gives three steps: borrow USDC against the gold you hold, buy more gold with it, pledge that gold for the next borrow — repeated to your multiplier. More gold means bigger gains, and bigger losses if gold falls. The slider runs 1.25× to 5× in 0.25 steps, with chips at 2×, 3×, 4× and 5×. The rest is fixed arithmetic: at multiplier m your loan-to-value is (m − 1) / m — 2× is 50%, 3× is 67%, 4× is 75%, 5× is 80%. Your commit is the only equity; everything above it is debt. Why people do it: they already wanted more gold at today's price and were short of cash. That is the whole case — a conviction trade, not a savings strategy. What you keep: title to all the gold. What you owe: the USDC plus interest, growing daily whatever gold does. What you could lose: the entire commit.

title: Boost — leverage
heading: Start with the loss, not the gain
text: One position, both directions, identical numbers. You commit US$10,000 of free gold at 3× . Auri borrows US$20,000 and buys more gold, so you hold US$30,000 of gold and owe US$20,000 at a 67% LTV. Gold falls 10%. Your gold is worth US$27,000; the debt is still US$20,000, because debt does not fall with the price. Equity is US$7,000 — you have lost US$3,000, 30% of your money , and your LTV is now 74%. Gold rises 10%. Gold US$33,000, debt US$20,000, equity US$13,000 — up US$3,000, or 30%. Unlevered. The same US$10,000 and the same 10% fall costs US$1,000. Before financing the two directions are symmetric; financing is not, since you pay it either way. And the loss column hides something: that 10% fall leaves you 3.8% from closure .
